title: Why are Arm Wrestlers so MONSTRUOUS?
summary: A narrated essay on why arm wrestlers develop such extreme physiques: the sport is a martial art built on technique, structure and highly specific strength, trained through table time and odd partial, heavy arm work. NH also covers widespread PED use in the untested heavyweight classes, genetics, the injury toll and the killer mindset of top pullers.
claims: Arm wrestling is a legitimate martial art: confrontation, risk of severe injury, technique, the ability to beat stronger opponents and lifelong practice
Arm wrestling needs a very specific strength you won't build with bench, squat and deadlift; it is a game of angles and leverage
Arm wrestling training ignores full range of motion and balanced development: you only train what you use, in table positions
John Brzenk reportedly avoided the gym and prepared by pulling at the table as much as possible
Bones and tendons matter as much as muscle because you pull with your structure; beginners in good clubs train only once a week to build resilience
The three key arm-wrestling qualities are rising, cupping and pronating, plus back and side pressure to finish
Arm wrestlers do in one day what bodybuilders do in a week of arm training, sometimes curling or holding close to bodyweight
Heavy partial preacher curls used by arm wrestlers build huge arms, contradicting the idea that only slow full-ROM reps grow biceps
Arm wrestlers are not meatheads; their specificity and handling of volume and intensity are top notch
Body mass matters in arm wrestling since many pins depend on how much weight you can hang on the opponent's arm
Arm wrestling is untested so PED use is rife, most obvious in the heavyweights who rival pro bodybuilders in size
Top pullers also have exceptional genetics, large bone structure and wrists; no drugs give you hands like Denis Cyplenkov
PEDs are less of a problem than in bodybuilding because size alone does not win; technique remains decisive
Pro arm wrestlers commonly undergo at least two major surgeries in their career, e.g. elbow or biceps tendon repair, and humerus fractures happen
